Brand name audit firms are global networks of local audit firms. These networks claim to enforce consistent audit methodologies across their member firms, which, if true, should systematically affect client financial reporting. We find that clients from different countries have more (less) comparable accruals when they are audited by local audit firms from the same global network (different global networks). Furthermore, inferences are similar when we examine client accrual comparability around audit firm switches induced by the failure of Andersen, which serves as a shock that helps improve identification. Results also suggest that the role of global network methodologies in global financial reporting comparability is more pronounced across stronger investor protection jurisdictions and across jurisdictions that have adopted International Standards on Auditing. audit firm networks, comparability, investor protection, ISAs. results.title: Audit market concentration, audit fees, and audit quality: A cross-country analysis of complex audit clients - ScienceDirect
results.content: However, academic research reaches different conclusions as several studies (e.g. Pearson and Trompeter, 1994, Feldman, 2006, Huang et al., 2016, Eshelman and Lawson, 2017) have provided evidence of a positive association between audit market concentration and audit fees. Some studies (Kallapur et al., 2010, Newton et al., 2013, Francis et al., 2013, Huang et al., 2016) have shown a positive association between overall (including Big 4 and non-Big 4) audit market concentration and audit quality, somewhat consistent with the sentiments of the General Accounting Office, 2003, Government Accountability Office, 2008 reports that increased concentration does not lead to decreased audit quality. Based on these considerations, we utilize a cross-country sample of audit client firms from 28 countries and find evidence of a positive association between Big 4 audit market concentration and audit fees for clients where the barriers to entry by competing auditors are likely higher (i.e. complex clients). Consistent with our expectations, we find that a positive association between Big 4 market concentration and audit fees exists for subsets of clients that are larger, exhibit international operations, and use IFRS. Early studies of audit concentration focus on the overall audit market in the U.S. and generally conclude that the audit market is characterized by price competition and concentration within the Big N group of auditors (Danos and Eichenseher, 1982, Doogar and Easley, 1998, Pearson and Trompeter, 1994). We provide evidence of such clients experiencing increased audit pricing while also experiencing lower quality in higher concentrated Big 4 audit markets. While results from research on the relation between market concentration and audit quality are unclear overall, our results suggest that concentration is associated with higher audit fees for larger and more complex audit engagements, at least within the Big 4 segment of the audit market. For example, the study of U.S. audit market concentration conducted by the General Accounting Office (2003) found no evidence of detrimental consequences to audit quality because of Big 4 market consolidation. Results indicate that audit fees charged to relatively complex clients are higher when the audit market is more heavily concentrated within the Big 4 group of auditors.

results.content: 3 Measures for CPA Firms to Improve Audit Quality and Ensure PCAOB Compliance. 4 How AcoBloom Can Help CPA Firms Ensure PCAOB Compliance and Improve Audit Quality. A PCAOB inspection is done to ascertain the audit firm’s adherence to PCAOB standards and rules & also to other rules and professional standards that are applicable to CPA firms in relation to its quality control and the areas of public company audits selected for PCAOB review. PCAOB will be maintaining or even increasing its oversight on CPA firms conducting assurance engagements for publicly listed entities, to ensure audit quality is maintained and CPA firms conduct stringent audit practices to ensure transparency and reliability on numbers presented in financial statements released by publicly traded entities. ## Measures for CPA Firms to Improve Audit Quality and Ensure PCAOB Compliance. The measures that CPA firm can take to improve quality and ensure compliance with PCAOB auditing standards and rules can be:. The outsourced audit process carries out detailed planning, execution and finalization of audits helping CPA firms to focus on critical areas of audits including review of audits leading to overall improvement of audit quality, and compliance with PCAOB Audit standards and rules. ## **How AcoBloom Can Help CPA Firms Ensure PCAOB Compliance and Improve Audit Quality**. The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) continues to elevate its oversight of CPA firms, demanding higher audit quality, transparency, and adherence to updated auditing standards. As the PCAOB prepares for heightened inspections in 2025, CPA firms must take proactive steps to address discrepancies highlighted in PCAOB inspection reports, including unsupported audit opinions, non-compliance with standards, independence issues, and quality control defects. By outsourcing non-core or non-critical tasks, CPA firms can allocate more resources to engagements requiring stringent PCAOB compliance, thereby improving audit quality and client satisfaction. The PCAOB’s rigorous inspection process underscores the need for CPA firms to enhance audit quality and compliance practices. By leveraging our expertise, CPA firms can ensure compliance with evolving PCAOB standards, maintain client confidence, and uphold their reputation in the competitive landscape of public company audits.

results.title: Legal Regimes' Influence on Audit Quality and Standards
results.content: Published Time: 2025-01-14T19:12:35+00:00 Legal Regimes’ Influence on Audit Quality and Standards - Accounting Insights #### Account Legal Regimes’ Influence on Audit Quality and Standards Explore how different legal frameworks shape audit quality, auditor independence, and liability, influencing global auditing standards. Audit quality and standards are vital for ensuring transparency and trust in financial reporting. Understanding the interplay between legal frameworks and audit quality directly impacts stakeholders’ confidence and the integrity of financial markets. This article explores how different legal systems affect audit quality, auditor independence, and liability, highlighting their role in maintaining robust auditing standards. Key Elements of Legal Regimes in Auditing Legal regimes in auditing are defined by statutes, regulations, and professional standards that establish the framework within which auditors operate. These standards provide a consistent basis for financial reporting, offering auditors a clear benchmark for assessing financial statements. For instance, the PCAOB’s Auditing Standard No. 5 emphasizes the importance of a robust control environment in auditing internal controls over financial reporting. Impact of Legal Regimes on Audit Quality The quality of audits depends heavily on the legal frameworks within which auditors operate. For instance, the PCAOB requires auditors to maintain detailed work papers to substantiate their audit opinions, ensuring audits are substantive inquiries into an organization’s financial health. For example, under IFRS, auditors must assess fair value measurements, balancing professional skepticism with adherence to legal standards. Auditor independence is fundamental to audit quality, ensuring audit opinions remain objective and reliable. Legal regimes establish frameworks to separate auditors from the entities they evaluate. Legal frameworks also restrict financial relationships between auditors and their clients to prevent conflicts of interest. These measures ensure a clear separation between the auditor’s interests and those of the client, bolstering trust in the audit process. By mandating openness, these legal stipulations strengthen stakeholder trust in the auditor’s objectivity and the reliability of financial statements. These frameworks determine the extent to which auditors are held accountable for their actions, emphasizing diligence and precision in audit execution. ##### Maintaining Ethical Standards in Accounting ##### Earnings Management: Techniques, Impact, and Detection ##### Addressing Biases in Auditing and Financial Analysis ##### What Are Internal Controls in Accounting and Why Are They Important?

results.title: PCAOB Publishes List of Issuer Audit Clients of Non-U.S. Registered Firms In Jurisdictions where the PCAOB is Denied Access To Conduct Inspections | PCAOB
results.content: Skip to Navigation Skip to Main Content Skip to Footer. # PCAOB Publishes List of Issuer Audit Clients of Non-U.S. Registered Firms In Jurisdictions where the PCAOB is Denied Access To Conduct Inspections. Washington, D.C., May 18, 2010. The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today published a list of more than 400 non-U.S. companies whose securities trade in U.S. markets, but whose PCAOB-registered auditors the Board currently cannot inspect because of asserted non-U.S. legal obstacles. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 requires auditors to be registered with, and regularly inspected by, the PCAOB if they audit the financial statements that issuers file with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). To date, the PCAOB has conducted more than 1,300 inspections of registered firms in the United States and 33 non-U.S. jurisdictions. PCAOB inspectors review – and focus firms on remedying deficiencies in – audit work relied on by investors in U.S. markets. Because investors in U.S. markets may be relying on the audit work of certain firms without realizing that those firms are presently uninspected by the PCAOB, the Board is publishing this list of issuers that have in 2009 or 2010 (through mid-April), filed financial statements with the SEC that were audited by a firm in one of these jurisdictions. The auditors of the issuers appearing on the list are located in China, Hong Kong, Switzerland and 18 European Union countries. The PCAOB continues to work to eliminate obstacles to inspections in these jurisdictions. * Issuer Audit Clients of Non-U.S. Registered Firms in Jurisdictions where the PCAOB is Denied Access to Conduct Inspections [*The list can be found under Related Information on the right side of the page*.]. ### Related Information. * Issuer Audit Clients of Non-U.S. Registered Firms in Jurisdictions where the PCAOB is Denied Access to Conduct Inspections.
